items: Miletus, on the coast of Asia. Ten generations have passed since the age of heroes ended.
In the hall of its princes — descendants of Nestor of Pylos — a singer has been summoned.
Sing for us, old father. Sing the great song — our fathers' fathers, and the war at Troy.
The great song is long, my lords. It does not begin at Troy.
It begins before Helen — before the heroes. It begins with the groaning of the Earth.
Muse, goddess of memory, sing through me —
— sing of the great wrath, of the long wanderings, of the burning of holy Wilios*, and of the hard roads home.
*Wilios, or Ilios — the city also called Troy; Wilusa in the treaties of the Hatti.
Begin where the gods began it.
Hear then, as the Muse gives it: how the plan of Zeus was set in motion.
In those days the generations of men had grown past all counting. Their kings warred, their cities multiplied, their weight lay heavy on the world.
And the Earth herself — mother of all living things — grew weary.
Zeus! Hear me! I am the Earth, mother of all living things!
The multitude of men is more than I can bear. Their cities crowd my plains; their wars tear my body; there is no rest left in me.
I do not ask for their destruction — they are my children. I ask for relief. Lighten my burden, Zeus, or I will break beneath it.
And Zeus was silent, weighing the fate of an age in his heart.
Then Zeus took counsel — not with his queen, nor with the gods at feast, but with Themis, the goddess of Right Order.
Once before, when mankind grew past all bearing, we sent the great flood. Not again — a flood is waste, and it teaches nothing.
Let it be a war. Let the age of heroes end as it has lived — in glory.
Then I will begin it with a quarrel among goddesses — and a judgment by a mortal man — and a woman so beautiful that every king will swear an oath for her sake.
And at Ilios, by the Hellespont, the finest of the heroes will fall — until Earth's burden is eased, and their names pass into song.
So the plan was made: death for the heroes, and undying glory with it.
Let it begin far from Troy, and years before it — in the two royal houses that will one day fight the war.
For the plan of Zeus does not strike like the thunderbolt. It grows slowly, like an oak — from old seed, planted in dark ground.
Now hear, princes, of the two old crimes from which your fathers' war grew. One was done at a table. One was done upon a wall.
In the west: the house of Tantalus — whom the gods loved too well.
In the east: the house of Laomedon — who cheated the gods of their wage.
Two debts owed to the gods. One reckoning to come. From these roots the war will grow.
No mortal was ever raised so high as Tantalus, king under Mount Sipylos. He sat at the gods' own table; nectar and ambrosia* passed his lips.
*Nectar and ambrosia — the drink and food of the gods, which keep them deathless.
But favor bred insolence. He stole the food of deathlessness for his table-companions below —
— and worse, he carried the counsels of the gods to mortal ears, to make himself great among men.
Tantalus had stolen from the gods and betrayed their secrets — and gone unpunished. So his pride grew, until he believed the deathless gods could be deceived by a mortal's cunning.
To test them, he did a deed the singer will name only once: he slew his own son, Pelops, and set the flesh before his guests as a feast — to see if they would know.
Abomination! Did you dream we would not know?
Restore the boy! And for you, Tantalus — a table is prepared in the world below!

The gods knew at once, and no dish was touched — save by one goddess, deep in mourning for a lost daughter, who tasted before she saw. The gods restored the boy whole and living. Only that one shoulder could not be made again — and in its place the Fates set gleaming ivory, the mark of his father's sin, carried all his days.
And in the house of Hades, Tantalus stands forever in water to his chin. He stoops to drink: the pool flees into black earth. He reaches for the boughs: the wind tosses them to the clouds.
Food and drink forever before him — and forever beyond his reach.
So ends the first debt, princes. Now for the son, Pelops — and the chariot-race that won a kingdom and a curse.
The boy grew into the fairest of men, and Poseidon*, who had loved him, gave him at parting a chariot swift as storm.
*Poseidon — god of the sea, of horses, and of earthquakes.
With it Pelops crossed the sea to woo Hippodamia, daughter of Oenomaus, king of Pisa by the Alpheios.
Thirteen suitors had come before him. Their heads were set on stakes before the gate.
For an oracle had told Oenomaus he would die by his daughter's husband — and so he raced each suitor to the Isthmus, and speared each one from behind.
Not this one too. O gods, not this one too.
But Hippodamia went by night to Myrtilus the charioteer, her father's servant, son of Hermes* — the only man whose hands touched the king's axles.
*Hermes — god of roads, heralds, and cunning; father of Myrtilus.
Take out the bronze pins from the king's wheels and set wax pins in their place. When I am king of Pisa, half the kingdom is yours — I swear it before Zeus, who hears all oaths.
Before Zeus, then, prince. Half the kingdom. The god has heard you — and so have I.
So the race was sold before it was run.
They raced for the altar of Poseidon at the Isthmus — the bride in the suitor's car, the father hunting behind with his spear, as twelve times before.
Faster, Myrtilus! The stranger's back makes thirteen — er, FOURTEEN!
a single jagged impact-line burst, no written sound-word.
Treachery... mine own... Then hear me, gods below — let Myrtilus die... by the hand of the man he served today!
And with the curse on his lips, the king of Pisa died.
My half of the kingdom, son of Tantalus. Pay me. You swore it before Zeus.
Shall I share my kingdom with the treachery that won it? You are my shame, charioteer — and shame is best drowned.
Zeus heard your oath, Pelops — now let him hear my curse! As you have betrayed me, let your own family betray one another!
Let your children kill their own blood, and serve one another such feasts, until the gods grow sick of the house of Pelops!
From that day, men have called that sea the Myrtoan, after Myrtilus. And Hermes, his father, did not forget.
Remember this cliff, princes. The curse thrown from it will climb back, generation by generation — and it climbs first to the table of Atreus.
Pelops's sons were Atreus and Thyestes. When the throne of golden Mycenae fell vacant, the city called for a son of Pelops — and the brothers' long hatred began.
Let him reign who can show the gods' own token!

The token was a lamb with golden fleece, born in Atreus's flocks and hidden away. But Atreus's own wife, Aerope, loved Thyestes in secret — and stole it for him. So Thyestes showed the sign, and claimed the throne.
Behold the sign, Mycenae! The gods choose ME!
Then Zeus answered with his own token, for Atreus: the sun stopped in heaven — and went backward, west to east, against its course. *(caption v2 — clarified causality per review)*
The heavens themselves un-say you, brother! Mycenae is MINE — and you are banished!

In exile Thyestes starved — and in time Atreus learned of Aerope and the stolen lamb — and of the betrayal in his own marriage-bed. Yet he sent word of pardon, and welcome, and a feast of reconciliation.
Rise, brother. What is past is past. Tonight you dine at my table.
Of what was served at that table, the singer will say only this: Thyestes's young sons had been summoned to the palace before him — and were not at the feast.
My sons — MY SONS! Monster! Kin-devourer of your own blood's blood —
Gods of the dark! Break this house! Let the line of Atreus be served as I was served!
Twice-cursed now — by Myrtilus's fall and Thyestes's feast — the house of Pelops shone on, golden and rotten at the root.
In exile a son was born to Thyestes: Aegisthus. He was nursed on one lesson only.
And was it repaid, father? The feast?
All debts in this song are repaid, child. That one waits for the conqueror of Troy, on the day he comes home... but I run before my horses. Turn we now east — across the sea, to the wall.

East across the Aegean, at the gate of the Hellespont where all the sea-roads meet, stood Troy — Wilios of the songs, Wilusa in the great king's treaties — westernmost jewel of the empire of the Hatti.
Her king in the old days was Laomedon. His story is the second root of the war — for the walls of Troy were built by gods... and never paid for.
In that age, for a fault against Zeus, Apollo and Poseidon were bound to serve a mortal man one full year for a wage. The man was Laomedon.
Poseidon raised the wall. Apollo kept the king's cattle on the ridges of Ida. And the wall they made, no host of men could break.
Faster, you two! A year runs out, and my wall wants its towers!
The wage for those two, majesty — reckoned at the year's end —

One short stretch only was built by mortal hands — the work of Aeacus, a pious mortal king who labored beside the gods. Mark that weaker stretch well, princes: the fate of Troy will pass through it. *(v2 — simplified)*
The year is served, king of Troy. The wall stands. Our wage.
Wage? For runaway hirelings of whom no city will speak? Here is your wage: be gone unbeaten!
And if you stand there glowering — I will bind your hands and feet, crop your ears with bronze, and sell you to the islands for what a mutilated slave will fetch!
Hear him, brother. He has said it with his own mouth, before witnesses.
I heard, brother. Let the sea answer him. Let the sun answer him.
And they were gone from the hall like light off bronze.
Then Apollo the far-shooter turned his silver bow on Troy, and plague walked the streets of the unpaid wall.
And Poseidon sent the salt flood, and out of the flood a monster of the deep, to devour the people of the shore.
The gods' price, majesty... is the king's own blood. The monster must have... your daughter. Hesione.
...Then the gods shall have her. Chain her to the rocks.
And Troy chained its princess to the rock at low tide — Hesione, who had done no wrong — and the city watched from the walls, and the sea began to move.
But that day there put in at the Trojan shore, homing from the country of the Amazons, the mightiest man of that age or any age.
The sea is standing up, Heracles.
So it is. And there is a girl in its road.
Stranger — that club, that bow — save her, and name your price!
I do not sell rescues, king. But a labor deserves a wage. My price is the divine white mares of your house — the deathless horses Zeus himself once gave to Troy. *(v2 — simplified)*
The divine mares! ...Done, and done, before witnesses!
Keep it, princess. It was never your debt being paid on that rock.
Your wage, hero: two fine horses of my stable.
These are not the mares of Tros.
The mares of Tros are Troy's holy things — not fee for a wandering strongman. Take these and my thanks... or take the road.
King of Troy — a god built your wall, and you cheated him. A man saved your child, and you cheat him too.
Keep the mares. Feed them well. I will come back for my wage — and your wall will not help you, because I know who built it... and I know where it was built by men.
So Laomedon cheated a second wage — first the gods', now the hero's — and laughed. He would soon learn how long such debts are remembered. *(v2 — simplified)*
Years later, Heracles came back for his wage — not with a great army, but with six ships, picked companions, and a debt to collect. *(v2 — simplified)*
To the wall! Not the gate — the WALL! Telamon — you remember the stretch I showed you?
The man-built stretch, son of Zeus! My father Aeacus laid those stones — I know his work! *(v2 — simplified)*
For Telamon was the son of Aeacus — the very mortal who had helped the gods build the wall. And a son knows where his father's work is weakest. *(v2 — simplified)*
And the wall the gods built was never broken. The wall men built broke — and Telamon of Salamis went through it first of all mankind.
But glory is a dangerous wage too. When Heracles saw another man take the first honor of the breach, the black mood of his line came upon him.
Stones for an altar! An altar to HERACLES THE GLORIOUS VICTOR — first of heroes, by whose might the wall is down!

And Heracles stood a moment... and laughed, and the black mood passed — for honor had been given its share. Mark the trick of it, princes: a wise friend can turn a hero's wrath aside. Later in this song you will see what happens when no such friend is near. *(v2 — simplified)*
Through the lower city to the palace hill the six ships' men drove them, and at the top there was nowhere left to be carried in a litter.
King of Troy. Two wages owed. Payment... in full.
Laomedon fell, and his sons with him — all his sons but one: Podarces, the youngest, too young for the war and too proud to run.
To Telamon, first through the wall, went the first prize of honor: Hesione the princess, whom he had seen at the rock and never ceased seeing.
Son of Aeacus. My captor and my lord. May a captive ask one gift?
My brother's life. I purchase it — with this veil, and all it is worth.
Sold, princess. Let all Troy witness: the boy is bought back from the spear.

Podarces the swift-footed no longer. From this day your name is your ransom, boy: PRIAMOS — "the purchased one." Reign in Troy, and remember what buys and what forfeits: the wage paid, and the wage withheld.

So Hesione of Troy sailed west to Salamis, a Trojan princess in an Achaean hall. There she bore Telamon a son: Teucer the archer — half-Trojan blood that would one day come BACK to Troy, in the ships of her enemies.
And in the ashes, Troy crowned its child. Priam the purchased rebuilt the walls — and where men's work had broken, men's work was set again, stone by stone, in the same fated stretch.
But a wall may be rebuilt, and a wage still owed. The gods' grievance was not buried with Laomedon. It waited — for the fullness of the plan of Zeus.
Thus the two roots, princes: the feast in the west, the wall in the east. From the one came Agamemnon and the curse of his house. From the other, Priam and the debt of his city.
And the Earth, father? Was her burden eased?
Not yet, child. As yet, not one hero had fallen. The scales of Zeus had only begun to move.
Tomorrow, if the Muse is willing: a wedding on a holy mountain — all the gods among the guests — and one goddess uninvited, with a golden apple in her hand.
"Two jars stand at the door-sill of Zeus: one holds evils, one holds blessings. To one man he gives of both mingled; to another, sorrow only — and no mortal chooses the ladle."
— after the words of Achilles to Priam, in the last book of the song of the wrath.
